source.title: Understanding Generalization in Adversarial Training via the Bias-Variance Decomposition
source.authors: Yaodong Yu; Zi-Tong Yang; Edgar Dobriban; Jacob Steinhardt; Yi Ma

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper varies network width and plots test error, an alternative-setting test of the model-size version. The plotted test-error result is not described numerically or in text.
record.gate_note: The paper's results on bias and variance as adversarial perturbation size changes do not measure the test-error curves named in the claim versions. The width-sweep test-error result is included as a figure-only row. Results about double descent cited from other work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The only result touching a claim version is a width sweep (WRN-28-1 to 20) of adversarially trained models on CIFAR10, which plots standard test error and MSE risk (Fig. 7/14). That makes it a new-setting test of V1, not T2. The text never describes the test-error or risk curve's shape, so no verdict can be drawn. The paper's main results are bias and variance as functions of adversarial radius ε, a different axis and construct from any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The authors conclude the following. In adversarial training, bias increases monotonically with ε and dominates risk. Variance is unimodal, peaking near the robust interpolation threshold. These properties rule out some conceptual models (low-dimensional box, fixed Gaussian noise) and point to dynamic training noise in high dimensions. Unlabeled data and pre-training reduce bias, while early stopping and wider models mainly reduce variance. They frame the variance peak as an inverse echo of width-wise double descent, and suggest a link to effective model complexity for future work.
record.recipe_differences: The paper sweeps width and plots test error, but does so for adversarially trained models at fixed perturbation radius rather than in the original standard-training setting.
record.method_sensitivity: The width sweep is for adversarial training on CIFAR10 at ε=8/255; the paper does not describe how test error changes across widths.

fits_no_version.finding: Under adversarial training, MSE variance is unimodal in ε, peaking near the robust interpolation threshold. Bias rises monotonically and dominates the risk. This holds across CIFAR10, CIFAR100, ImageNet10, ℓ2/ℓ∞ attacks, randomized smoothing and high-dimensional synthetic models, but not for fixed Gaussian-noise training or low-dimensional box data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Variance (not test error) peaks at the interpolation threshold along a regularisation-strength axis (adversarial radius), mirroring the width-wise unimodal variance.

fits_no_version.finding: In the width sweep under adversarial training, bias decreases monotonically with width. Variance increases up to the robust interpolation threshold (width=4), then changes little.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bias/variance decomposition along model width in adversarial training.

fits_no_version.finding: Evaluated on CIFAR10-C, variance over ε becomes 'double-descent-shaped' (two dips) and bias becomes U-shaped (Fig. 15).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multiple-peak variance curves over adversarial radius under distribution shift.

record.problems: The width-sweep test-error result is presented only in a plot, without a textual characterization or reported numeric values; the text therefore does not establish whether the test-error curve has the claimed shape.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant test-error outcomes are stated. Bias/variance results over perturbation size and width are not test-error results; cited double-descent findings are from other work.

untested.parts: Standard (non-adversarial) training; any stated or numeric test-error curve over width; noise conditions; architectures beyond WRN-28.
Not tested; no test-error-over-epochs curve, and early stopping is a single epoch-100 snapshot.
Not tested; logistic-regression and box experiments sweep ε and report bias/variance, not risk versus capacity.
Only speculated in the Discussion (an 'effective model complexity' link); no measure is defined or tested.
Not tested; there are no label-noise or regularisation-tuning sweeps of test error.

missing.what: Text-stated bias/variance trends over width: bias monotonically decreasing; variance rising until width=4 (the robust interpolation threshold), then roughly flat. These are needed to interpret r1, though they are not test error.
missing.locator: Appendix C.2, 'Effect of width factor'; Figure 14; Section 5 'Model width'

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts are given: the only V1-relevant row is figure-only, with no textual description of the test-error shape. The tranche was changed from T2 to T3 because the width sweep is in a new setting (adversarial training), not an alternative method on standard training. The study is not an original source. A reader of Figure 7/14 could add a value for r1.

versions.untested_parts: Only a width sweep of adversarially trained WRN-28-[width] at fixed ε=8/255 is plotted. The test-error curve is not described in text or given numerically; the paper does not test standard training settings.

rows.subject: WideResNet-28-[width]
rows.operation_detail: Varied network width factor while holding adversarial-training ε fixed.
rows.note: The text says test error was evaluated across width factors but does not characterize its curve. The appendix text describes bias and variance over width, not the test-error trend.
rows.check: Setting is adversarial training (ℓ∞, ε=8/255), a new setting rather than an alternative method, so the tranche should be T3. The test-error and risk curves over width are figure-only and uncharacterised in the text. The appendix describes only bias (monotonically decreasing) and variance (rising to width=4, then roughly flat). That does not establish a fall-rise-fall in test error.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
